title: Medieval Indian History
summary: From the tripartite struggle to the Third Battle of Panipat: Delhi Sultanate reforms, Vijayanagara and the Deccan sultanates, the Mughals and Sher Shah, Marathas, Sikh Gurus, Bhakti–Sufi saints, and the books and travellers of the period. SSC asks 1–2 questions per shift, nearly always a pairing (ruler–reform, battle–year, book–author, traveller–ruler), so the tables here cover most of them.

subtopics.title: Early Medieval India (c. 750–1206)
subtopics.concept:
**Basics you must know**

| Point | Fact |
|---|---|
| Tripartite struggle | 8th–10th century fight for **Kannauj** between the **Palas** (Bengal), **Gurjara-Pratiharas** (western India) and **Rashtrakutas** (Deccan) |
| Palas | Founded by **Gopala** (c. 750, "elected" by chiefs); **Dharmapala** revived **Nalanda** and founded **Vikramashila** university |
| Gurjara-Pratiharas | **Nagabhata I** checked Arab advance; **Mihira Bhoja** (Adivaraha coins) is the best-known ruler |
| Rashtrakutas | Founder **Dantidurga**; capital **Manyakheta**; **Amoghavarsha I** wrote *Kavirajamarga* (Kannada) |
| Arab conquest of Sindh | **Muhammad bin Qasim**, **712 CE**, defeated **Raja Dahir** |
| Mahmud of Ghazni | **17 raids** (1000–1027); sacked **Somnath** temple (1025); scholar **Al-Biruni** came with him and wrote *Kitab-ul-Hind* |
| Muhammad Ghori | **First Battle of Tarain 1191** – lost to **Prithviraj Chauhan**; **Second Battle of Tarain 1192** – won; **Chandawar 1194** – defeated **Jaichand** (Gahadavala, Kannauj) |
| Kashmir chronicle | **Kalhana's *Rajatarangini*** (12th c.) — first proper historical work in Sanskrit |
| Chand Bardai | Court poet of Prithviraj; *Prithviraj Raso* |

**Rajput dynasties (quick map)**

| Dynasty | Region | Remember for |
|---|---|---|
| Chauhans (Chahamanas) | Ajmer–Delhi | Prithviraj III |
| Gahadavalas | Kannauj–Varanasi | Jaichand |
| Paramaras | Malwa (Dhar) | **Raja Bhoja** — scholar-king, Bhojpur |
| Chandelas | Bundelkhand | **Khajuraho** temples |
| Solankis (Chalukyas of Gujarat) | Gujarat | Dilwara (Mt Abu) & Modhera Sun temple era |
| Tomaras | Delhi region | Founded **Dhillika** (Delhi) |

tricks.title: Tripartite = "PPR fight for K"
tricks.body: **P**ala, **P**ratihara, **R**ashtrakuta → **K**annauj. East, West and South all wanted the centre.

example.q: Which of these dynasties was NOT part of the tripartite struggle — Pala, Pratihara, Chola, Rashtrakuta?
example.solution: **Chola** — the three were Pala, Pratihara and Rashtrakuta.

tricks.title: Tarain: 1 to Prithviraj, 2 to Ghori
tricks.body: **1191 → 1st** battle → Prithviraj wins. **1192 → 2nd** battle → Ghori wins. The second number always goes to the invader.

mistakes: Somnath was raided by **Mahmud of Ghazni** (1025), not Muhammad Ghori.
Al-Biruni came with **Mahmud of Ghazni**; Ibn Battuta came under **Muhammad bin Tughlaq**.
Arab conquest of Sindh (712) was by **Muhammad bin Qasim**, not Mahmud.
subtopics.notes:
### After Harsha: a mosaic of kingdoms
From the 8th century north India split among the **Palas** (Bengal-Bihar), the **Gurjara-Pratiharas** (Malwa-Rajasthan) and the **Rashtrakutas** (Deccan), all three fighting for **Kannauj** — the famous **tripartite struggle**. The **Palas** began when **Gopala** was elected king (c. 750); **Dharmapala** founded the **Vikramashila** monastery and revived Nalanda, and the dynasty patronised Buddhism. The Pratiharas under **Nagabhata I** turned back Arab raids; **Mihira Bhoja** was their best-known ruler. The Rashtrakutas (founder **Dantidurga**) gave India the **Kailasa temple, Ellora (Krishna I)** and the *Kavirajamarga* (Amoghavarsha). Rajput clans filled the rest of the north: the **Chauhans** (Delhi-Ajmer — **Prithviraj III**, the two Battles of **Tarain**, 1191 and 1192), **Gahadavalas** (Kannauj — Jaichand), **Paramaras** (Malwa — the scholar-king **Bhoja** of Dhara), **Chandellas** (Khajuraho temples), **Solankis** (Somnath, Dilwara), and the **Senas** of Bengal (Lakshmanasena, the last old-order king, whose capital fell to Bakhtiyar Khalji).

### The Cholas at their height
The imperial line began when **Vijayalaya** captured **Thanjavur** (c. 850). **Rajaraja I** conquered Sri Lanka and the Maldives and built the great **Brihadeshwara (Rajarajeshwara) temple at Thanjavur**. His son **Rajendra I** marched to the Ganga (taking the title **Gangaikonda**, and building the capital **Gangaikondacholapuram**) and sent a **naval expedition against Srivijaya** (Shailendra kingdom of Sumatra-Malaya peninsula) to guard the China trade. The Chola navy, the bronzes (**Nataraja**) and temple building mark the age's peak.

### Village self-rule: the Uttaramerur inscriptions
The Cholas' most-quoted contribution is **local self-government**. The **Uttaramerur inscriptions** (of **Parantaka I**'s reign) record how village committees (**variyams**) were chosen by the **kudavolai** (pot-ticket) system — candidates were screened for age, property and learning, names were drawn from a pot, and members could be removed for misconduct. Village assemblies had three forms: the **ur** (common villages), the **sabha** (Brahmadeya, Brahmana-grant villages) and the **nagaram** (merchant towns).

### Other regional powers
Eastern **Gangas** of Odisha — **Narasimhadeva I** built the **Konark Sun Temple**. **Hoysalas** (capital **Dorasamudra/Halebidu**, temples at Belur-Halebidu-Somnathpura). **Kakatiyas** of Warangal — ruled briefly by the woman ruler **Rani Rudramadevi**. **Western Chalukyas of Kalyani** (Vikramaditya VI) fought the Cholas for the Tungabhadra doab; **Yadavas** held Devagiri until Alauddin Khalji's raids.

### Quick revision
- Tripartite struggle = Pala vs Pratihara vs Rashtrakuta, prize **Kannauj**; Gopala = elected Pala founder; Dharmapala = Vikramashila.
- Rajput houses: Chauhan-Prithviraj (Tarain 1191/1192), Paramara-Bhoja, Chandella-Khajuraho, Solanki-Somnath, Gahadavala-Jaichand, Sena-Lakshmanasena.
- Chola chain: Vijayalaya (850, Thanjavur) → Rajaraja I (Brihadeshwara) → Rajendra I (Gangaikonda; navy vs Srivijaya).
- Uttaramerur (Parantaka I): kudavolai lottery, variyam committees; assemblies = ur, sabha, nagaram.
- Regional capitals: Hoysala-Dorasamudra, Kakatiya-Warangal, Ganga-Konark.

patterns.name: Tripartite struggle and the three powers
patterns.howToSpot: 'Who won the tripartite struggle', Pala-Pratihara-Rashtrakuta founder or university or temple links.
patterns.logic:
1. Powers: **Palas = Bengal-Bihar (Buddhist)**, Gurjara-Pratiharas = Malwa-Rajasthan, Rashtrakutas = Deccan; prize = **Kannauj**.
2. Anchors: Gopala (elected Pala), Dharmapala (Vikramashila), Nagabhata I (Arab raids), Krishna I (Kailasa Ellora), Amoghavarsha (Kavirajamarga).
3. In statement questions, check which dynasty each fact belongs to before judging.

example.q: Which Pala ruler founded the **Vikramashila** monastery?
example.solution: **Dharmapala** — the Palas were the great Buddhist patrons of Bengal-Bihar.

patterns.name: Chola rulers ↔ achievements
patterns.howToSpot: 'Gangaikonda was the title of', who built the Brihadeshwara temple, the naval expedition against Srivijaya, order of Chola rulers.
patterns.logic:
1. Chain: Vijayalaya (founder, Thanjavur) → Rajaraja I → Rajendra I.
2. Rajaraja I = **Brihadeshwara temple, Thanjavur**; Rajendra I = **Gangaikonda** title, **Gangaikondacholapuram**, **navy vs Srivijaya (Shailendra)**.
3. The Srivijaya raid was to protect the **China trade route** — a favourite 'why' question.

example.q: Which Chola ruler sent a naval expedition against the **Srivijaya** kingdom?
example.solution: **Rajendra I** — to secure the sea route to China; he also marched to the Ganga (title Gangaikonda).

patterns.name: Chola village administration: Uttaramerur and kudavolai
patterns.howToSpot: 'The kudavolai system', which inscription records village committees, ur vs sabha vs nagaram, eligibility rules.
patterns.logic:
1. Source: **Uttaramerur inscriptions**, reign of **Parantaka I**.
2. System: **kudavolai (pot-ticket)** — names drawn from a pot; committees called **variyam**; eligibility rules on age, property, learning.
3. Assemblies: **ur** = common villages, **sabha** = Brahmadeya (Brahmana) villages, **nagaram** = merchant towns.

example.q: Under the **kudavolai** system of the Cholas, village committee members were chosen by —
example.solution: Drawing **lots (tickets) from a pot** — hence 'pot-ticket' — under rules recorded in the Uttaramerur inscriptions.

patterns.name: Rajput and regional kingdoms: houses ↔ capitals & rulers
patterns.howToSpot: 'Which dynasty ruled Warangal', 'Rani Rudramadevi belonged to', Konark-Halebidu-Khajuraho builder links, Tarain facts.
patterns.logic:
1. Houses: Chauhan-Delhi-Ajmer (Prithviraj, Tarain), Paramara-Malwa (Bhoja), Chandella-Khajuraho, Solanki-Gujarat (Somnath), Gahadavala-Kannauj (Jaichand), Sena-Bengal (Lakshmanasena).
2. Deccan-south: Kakatiya-Warangal (Rudramadevi), Hoysala-Dorasamudra (Belur-Halebidu), Eastern Ganga-Odisha (Narasimhadeva I, Konark).
3. Match the temple to its builder-dynasty before answering.

example.q: **Rani Rudramadevi**, a rare woman ruler of the medieval age, belonged to which dynasty?
example.solution: The **Kakatiyas** of Warangal (Telangana-Andhra).

subtopics.title: Delhi Sultanate (1206–1526)
subtopics.concept:
**Five dynasties in order**

| Dynasty | Years | Founder |
|---|---|---|
| Mamluk / Slave (Ilbari) | 1206–1290 | **Qutb-ud-din Aibak** |
| Khalji | 1290–1320 | **Jalal-ud-din Khalji** |
| Tughlaq | 1320–1414 | **Ghiyas-ud-din Tughlaq** |
| Sayyid | 1414–1451 | Khizr Khan |
| Lodi (only Afghan dynasty) | 1451–1526 | **Bahlol Lodi** |

**Ruler → signature fact (most asked)**

| Ruler | What SSC asks |
|---|---|
| **Qutb-ud-din Aibak** | "Lakh Baksh" (generous giver); began **Qutub Minar**; Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque (Delhi) & Adhai Din ka Jhonpra (Ajmer); died falling from horse playing **chaugan (polo)** 1210; capital **Lahore** |
| **Iltutmish** | Real consolidator; shifted capital to **Delhi**; **iqta** system; **Turkan-i-Chahalgani** (Group of Forty); pure Arabic coins — silver **tanka** & copper **jital**; completed Qutub Minar; investiture from Abbasid Caliph (1229) |
| **Razia Sultan** | First and only woman ruler of Delhi (1236–40); daughter of Iltutmish |
| **Balban** | "Blood and iron" policy; **sijda** (prostration) and **paibos** (kissing feet); Persian festival **Nauroz**; created **Diwan-i-Arz** (military dept); crushed the Chahalgani |
| **Alauddin Khalji** | **Market control** (Shahna-i-Mandi, price fixing); **dagh** (branding horses) & **chehra** (descriptive roll of soldiers); standing army paid in cash; land revenue **50%**; **Alai Darwaza** (1311), Siri Fort; general **Malik Kafur** raided the south |
| **Ghiyas-ud-din Tughlaq** | Built **Tughlaqabad**; died when a pavilion collapsed (1325) |
| **Muhammad bin Tughlaq** | Capital to **Daulatabad (Devagiri) 1327**; **token currency** in bronze/copper (1329–30); **Diwan-i-Amir-Kohi** (agriculture dept); Moroccan traveller **Ibn Battuta** was his qazi of Delhi |
| **Firoz Shah Tughlaq** | Canals (Yamuna, Sutlej); **Diwan-i-Khairat** (charity), **Diwan-i-Bandagan** (slaves); jizya extended to Brahmins; founded Firozabad, Hisar, Jaunpur; brought **Ashokan pillars** from Topra and Meerut to Delhi |
| Timur's invasion | **1398**, under Nasir-ud-din Mahmud Tughlaq |
| **Sikandar Lodi** | Founded **Agra (1504)**; **Gaz-i-Sikandari** (measuring yard); pen-name *Gulrukhi* |
| **Ibrahim Lodi** | Last Sultan; killed at **First Battle of Panipat, 1526** |

**Historians of the Sultanate:** Minhaj-us-Siraj – *Tabaqat-i-Nasiri*; **Ziauddin Barani** – *Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi*, *Fatawa-i-Jahandari*; Amir Khusrau – *Khazain-ul-Futuh*, *Tughlaqnama*.

tricks.title: Dynasty order — "Sabka Khana Tum Sab Lo"

example.q: Which dynasty ruled Delhi immediately before the Lodis?
example.solution: Tum **Sab** Lo → **Sayyid** comes just before Lodi.

tricks.title: Who did what — first letter hooks
tricks.body: **I**ltutmish = **I**qta + **I**nvestiture; **B**alban = **B**ow down (sijda/paibos); **A**lauddin = **A**ll prices fixed; **M**uhammad bin Tughlaq = **M**ove capital + **M**oney tokens; **F**iroz = **F**ields & canals.

mistakes: Token currency and Daulatabad = **Muhammad bin Tughlaq**, not Firoz Shah.
Market control = **Alauddin Khalji**; Balban never fixed prices.
Qutub Minar was **begun** by Aibak but **completed** by Iltutmish.
The Lodis were **Afghans**; all earlier Sultanate dynasties were Turkish (the Sayyids claimed descent from the Prophet).
subtopics.notes:
### Five dynasties, 320 years (1206–1526)
| Dynasty | Period | Remember |
|---|---|---|
| **Slave (Mamluk/Ilbari)** | 1206–1290 | Qutbuddin Aibak founded; Iltutmish consolidated; Razia (only woman); Balban (kingship theory) |
| **Khalji** | 1290–1320 | Alauddin: market control, standing army, southern raids |
| **Tughlaq** | 1320–1414 | MBT's experiments; Firoz Shah's works |
| **Sayyid** | 1414–1451 | Khizr Khan (after Timur's sack) |
| **Lodi** | 1451–1526 | First Afghan house; Ibrahim Lodi fell at Panipat 1526 |

**Iltutmish** (real founder) introduced the **silver tanka** and copper **jital**, completed the Qutub Minar, and formed the **Chahalgani ('the Forty')** group of Turani nobles. **Balban** stressed royal dignity — **sijda** and **paibos** — and ruled by 'blood and iron'. **Alauddin Khalji** ran a **standing army** (soldiers identified by **chehra** descriptive rolls, horses by **daag** branding), fixed **market prices** (Shahna-i-Mandi supervising), and sent **Malik Kafur** into the far south. **Muhammad bin Tughlaq** tried the **capital shift to Daulatabad** and **token copper currency** (forged, and failed). **Firoz Shah Tughlaq** built canals, rest houses, Diwan-i-Khairat (charity) and Diwan-i-Bandagan (slaves), and **extended jizya to Brahmanas**. **Timur's** sack of Delhi (**1398**) broke the Tughlaqs; the Lodis' **Sikandar** founded **Agra**, and **Ibrahim Lodi** lost to Babur at **Panipat (1526)** — the Sultanate's end.

### The machinery of the state
- **Iqta system:** revenue assignments (**iqta**) to nobles (**muqti/iqtadar**) who collected tax and kept troops — the Sultanate's revenue-military base.
- **Diwans:** **Wizarat** (finance), **Ariz** (military), **Risalat** (foreign/religious), **Qaza** (justice), **Insha** (correspondence).
- **Barids and munihiyan:** intelligence and secret agents. The ulema's opinion weighed in state matters; Persian was the court language.

### Economy and society
Land tax (**kharaj**) could reach a third to a half of produce; **jizya** fell on non-Muslims (as a state practice from Firoz Shah, on Brahmanas too). Craft and markets thrived (Alauddin's price control is the classic case); Persianate culture, calligraphy and mosque-arch architecture (arch and dome, Alai Darwaza, Tughlaq sloping walls) took root.

### Quick revision
- Dynasty ladder: Slave 1206 → Khalji 1290 → Tughlaq 1320 → Sayyid 1414 → Lodi 1451 → ends 1526 (Panipat).
- Iltutmish: tanka-jital, Chahalgani, Qutub Minar; Balban: sijda-paibos, blood & iron.
- Alauddin: chehra-daag, market reforms (Shahna-i-Mandi), Malik Kafur's southern raids, Siri.
- MBT: Daulatabad shift + token currency (both failed); Firoz Shah: canals, charity departments, jizya on Brahmanas.
- Iqta = revenue-for-service; Diwan-i-Ariz = army; Timur 1398 → Sayyids; 1526 ends it all.

patterns.name: Dynasty ↔ founder ↔ landmark chain
patterns.howToSpot: 'Which dynasty ruled when', founder questions, Razia as first woman ruler, 'the Forty'.
patterns.logic:
1. Ladder with dates: Slave 1206, Khalji 1290, Tughlaq 1320, Sayyid 1414, Lodi 1451, end 1526.
2. Anchors: Aibak founded, Iltutmish consolidated (tanka, Forty), Razia = first and only woman sultan, Balban = blood & iron.
3. Sayyids came after Timur's 1398 sack; Lodis were the first Afghan house.

example.q: The group of forty leading slaves of Iltutmish, which dominated court politics, was called —
example.solution: **Chahalgani (Turkan-i-Chihalgani), 'the Forty'** — it set up and pulled down sultans after Iltutmish.

patterns.name: Administration and economy: iqta, diwans, market control
patterns.howToSpot: 'The iqta system meant', Diwan-i-Ariz/Wizarat functions, chehra-daag, price control machinery, kharaj-jizya.
patterns.logic:
1. **Iqta**: revenue assignment to a muqti in return for troops and service — not ownership.
2. Diwans: **Wizarat = finance**, **Ariz = army**, **Risalat = foreign/religious**, **Qaza = justice**, **Insha = correspondence**.
3. Alauddin's army tools: **chehra** (descriptive roll), **daag** (horse branding); market control under the **Shahna-i-Mandi**.

example.q: Which department of the Delhi Sultanate looked after the **army**?
example.solution: **Diwan-i-Ariz** — the military department (headed by the Ariz-i-Mumalik).

patterns.name: Sultans' landmark acts and famous experiments
patterns.howToSpot: Daulatabad shift, token currency, canals and charity departments of Firoz Shah, jizya extensions, Qutub Minar.
patterns.logic:
1. MBT's pair of failures: **Daulatabad capital shift** and **token copper currency** (forgery killed it); also Khorasan and Qarachil expeditions.
2. Firoz Shah: **canals**, Diwan-i-Khairat & Diwan-i-Bandagan, Firoz Shah Kotla, and **jizya extended to Brahmanas**.
3. Qutub Minar begun by Aibak, completed by Iltutmish.

example.q: Muhammad bin Tughlaq's **token currency** failed mainly because —
example.solution: **Copper tokens were easily forged** by the public; the treasury had to redeem them at face value, and the scheme was withdrawn.

patterns.name: Foreign invasions and the Sultanate's end
patterns.howToSpot: Mongol threat and Siri, Timur's sack and the Sayyids, Bakhtiyar Khalji in Bihar-Bengal, First Battle of Panipat.
patterns.logic:
1. Mongols: repelled by Balban's stern policy; **Alauddin built Siri** and met them at the gates of Delhi.
2. **Timur, 1398** — sacked Delhi, ended Tughlaq power, led to the Sayyids.
3. **1526, First Battle of Panipat** — Babur beat Ibrahim Lodi; Sultanate ends, Mughals begin.

example.q: Which sultan built the **fort of Siri** as a shelter against the Mongols?
example.solution: **Alauddin Khalji** — Mongol invasions pressed Delhi repeatedly in his reign.

subtopics.title: Vijayanagara & Bahmani Kingdoms
subtopics.concept:
**Vijayanagara empire (1336–1646)**

| Point | Fact |
|---|---|
| Founded | **1336** by brothers **Harihara I and Bukka Raya** (Sangama dynasty); capital **Hampi** on the **Tungabhadra** |
| Four dynasties | **Sangama → Saluva → Tuluva → Aravidu** |
| Greatest ruler | **Krishnadevaraya** (Tuluva, 1509–29) — wrote Telugu poem ***Amuktamalyada***; court of **Ashtadiggajas** (eight poets) incl. **Allasani Peddana** and **Tenali Ramakrishna** |
| Decline | **Battle of Talikota (Rakshasi–Tangadi), 1565** — Rama Raya killed by the combined Deccan sultanates |
| Heritage | Group of Monuments at **Hampi** — UNESCO site (1986); Vitthala temple stone chariot |

**Foreign visitors to Vijayanagara**

| Visitor | From | Ruler |
|---|---|---|
| Niccolo de Conti | Italy | Deva Raya I |
| **Abdur Razzaq** | Persia (Timurid envoy) | **Deva Raya II** |
| **Domingo Paes** | Portugal | **Krishnadevaraya** |
| Fernao Nuniz | Portugal | Achyuta Raya |

**Bahmani kingdom (1347–1527)**
- Founded **1347** by **Alauddin Hasan Bahman Shah (Hasan Gangu)**; capital **Gulbarga**, later **Bidar**.
- Minister **Mahmud Gawan** built a famous **madrasa at Bidar**.
- Split into **five Deccan Sultanates**:

| Sultanate | Dynasty | Monument to remember |
|---|---|---|
| **Bijapur** | Adil Shahi | **Gol Gumbaz** (Muhammad Adil Shah) — whispering gallery |
| **Golconda** | Qutb Shahi | **Charminar**, Hyderabad (1591, Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah) |
| **Ahmadnagar** | Nizam Shahi | Chand Bibi resisted Akbar |
| **Bidar** | Barid Shahi | — |
| **Berar** | Imad Shahi | Did **not** join the Talikota alliance |

tricks.title: Vijayanagara dynasties — "Some Silly Tigers Attack"
tricks.body: **S**angama → **S**aluva → **T**uluva → **A**ravidu. Krishnadevaraya sits in the third (**T**uluva — "Top king").

example.q: Krishnadevaraya belonged to which dynasty of Vijayanagara?
example.solution: Top king → **T**uluva dynasty.

tricks.title: Deccan five — "BiG AB B"
tricks.body: **Bi**japur (Adil), **G**olconda (Qutb), **A**hmadnagar (Nizam), **B**idar (Barid), **B**erar (Imad). The first letters of the dynasty names: A-Q-N-B-I.

mistakes: Hampi is on the **Tungabhadra**, not the Krishna.
Abdur Razzaq visited **Deva Raya II**, not Krishnadevaraya.
Gol Gumbaz is in **Bijapur**; Charminar is in **Hyderabad** (Golconda kingdom).
subtopics.notes:
### City of victory on the Tungabhadra
**Vijayanagara** ('city of victory') was founded in **1336** on the Tungabhadra bank at **Hampi** by the Sangama brothers **Harihara and Bukka**, blessed by the guru **Vidyaranya**. Four dynasties ruled it in turn: **Sangama → Saluva → Tuluva → Aravidu**. Its economy rested on the fertile **Raichur doab** (the doab of the Krishna-Tungabhra rivers, long contested with the Bahmanis), diamond and spice trade, and a powerful cavalry fed by Portuguese horse imports.

### Krishnadevaraya, the greatest ruler (1509–1529)
Of the **Tuluva** dynasty, he defeated the Bahmanis and the Odisha (Gajapati) king, and won the **Battle of Raichur** (1520, with Portuguese muskets). Titles: **Andhra Bhoja**, 'establisher of Yavana rule' and more. His court had the **Ashtadiggajas** (eight elephants of learning), the greatest being **Allasani Peddana** (*Manucharitam*, honoured as 'Andhra Kavita Pitamaha'); Krishnadevaraya himself wrote the Telugu classic **Amuktamalyada**. Portuguese visitors **Domingo Paes** and **Duarte Barbosa** describe his glittering capital — the **Virupaksha** and **Vittala** temples (the famous stone chariot), the Hazara Rama temple, and bazaars of pearls.

### The Bahmani kingdom and its five heirs
The **Bahmani kingdom** was founded in **1347** by **Alauddin Hasan Bahman Shah (Hasan Gangu)** with its capital at **Gulbarga** (later **Bidar**). Its able wazir **Mahmud Gawan** was executed by court factions (1481) — after which the kingdom split into **five sultanates**: **Bijapur (Adil Shahi), Ahmadnagar (Nizam Shahi), Golconda (Qutb Shahi), Berar (Imad Shahi) and Bidar (Barid Shahi)**.

### Rivalry and the fall
Vijayanagara and the Bahmanis fought almost continuously over the Raichur doab, the Krishna-Godavara delta and horse trade. In **1565**, at the **Battle of Talikota (Rakshasa-Tangadi)**, a coalition of the Deccan sultanates crushed Vijayanagara; the de facto ruler **Rama Raya** (Aravidu) was captured and executed, and Hampi was sacked and abandoned. The dynasty lingered from Penukonda-Chandragiri; Nayak kingdoms took over the south. The ruins are the **Hampi** UNESCO World Heritage site — 'a city of victory in stone'.

### Quick revision
- 1336, Harihara-Bukka (Sangama), guru Vidyaranya; dynasties Sangama-Saluva-Tuluva-Aravidu.
- Krishnadevaraya (Tuluva): Raichur win, Ashtadiggajas, Allasani Peddana, Amuktamalyada, visitor Paes.
- Bahmani: Hasan Gangu, 1347, Gulbarga → Bidar; Mahmud Gawan executed; five sultanates (B-A-G-B-B).
- 1565 Talikota: five sultanates beat Rama Raya; Hampi sacked; today = UNESCO site.

patterns.name: Vijayanagara: founders and the four dynasties
patterns.howToSpot: 'Who founded Vijayanagara and when', which dynasty Krishnadevaraya belonged to, guru Vidyaranya, order of dynasties.

example.solution: **Sher Shah Suri** (and his Sur successors), 1540–1555.

tricks.title: Three Panipats — 26, 56, 61
tricks.body: **1526** Babur beats Ibrahim Lodi · **1556** Akbar (Bairam Khan) beats Hemu · **1761** Ahmad Shah Abdali beats the Marathas. Gap pattern: +30 years, then +205 years.

mistakes: Rupiya was introduced by **Sher Shah**, not Akbar.
Din-i-Ilahi = **1582**, Ibadat Khana = **1575** — do not swap.
Haldighati Mughal commander = **Man Singh**, not Akbar in person.
Taj Mahal = Shah Jahan; Itimad-ud-Daulah = **Nur Jahan**.
subtopics.notes:
### Founding the empire (1526–1556)
**Babur**, a Chagatai Timurid from Fergana, won the **First Battle of Panipat (1526)** against **Ibrahim Lodi** using artillery and the *tulughma* encircling tactics. In **1527** he beat **Rana Sanga** of Mewar at **Khanwa**; Chanderi followed (1528). His memoir, the **Baburnama (Tuzuk-i-Baburi)**, is in **Turkish** — a candid classic. **Humayun** lost the empire to **Sher Shah Sur** at **Chausa (1539)** and **Kannauj (1540)**, wandered 15 years (Persia's help), returned in 1555, and died within months.
### Sher Shah Sur (1540–1545), the gap-filler
An Afghan of Sasaram, Sher Shah ran the empire better than many kings: he issued the **rupiya** (silver) and dam (copper), rebuilt the **Grand Trunk Road** (Sonargaon in Bengal to the north-west) with **sarais** at stages, standardised **patta** (title deed) and **qabuliyat** (deed of agreement) in revenue, and organized a spy-run administration. His tomb at **Sasaram** is a landmark.
### Akbar (1556–1605): the empire takes shape
Regent **Bairam Khan** won the **Second Battle of Panipat (1556)** over **Hemu**. Akbar then: conquered Malwa, Chittor (1568) and Ranthambhor, Gujarat and Bengal; pursued a **Rajput policy of alliance** (marriages with Amber's house; Raja Man Singh and Todar Mal in high service); abolished the **pilgrimage tax** and **jizya**; and built **Fatehpur Sikri** with the **Buland Darwaza**. Finance minister **Raja Todar Mal** set the **dahsala (zabti) system** — revenue fixed on a 10-year average. The **mansabdari** system graded officers by **zat** (personal rank) and **sawar** (cavalry). In 1582 he promulgated **Din-i-Ilahi**, a syncretic order; **Ibadat Khana** at Fatehpur Sikri hosted debates. The **Navaratna** circle: Birbal, Todar Mal, Abul Fazl, Faizi, Tansen, Man Singh and others.
### Jahangir, Shah Jahan, Aurangzeb
**Jahangir** (1605–27): the 'chain of justice', paintings peak, **Sir Thomas Roe** (James I's ambassador, 1615); **Nur Jahan** ran the court. **Shah Jahan** (1628–58): the **Peacock Throne (Takht-i-Taus)**, **Taj Mahal** (for **Mumtaz Mahal**), Red Fort, Jama Masjid — the monument age. **Aurangzeb** (1658–1707): reimposed **jizya (1679)**, executed **Guru Tegh Bahadur (1675)**, fought the Marathas for 25 years in the Deccan — the drain that hollowed the empire.
### Later Mughals
Successors were puppets (the **Sayyid brothers** as king-makers). **Nadir Shah's** invasion (1739, **Battle of Karnal**) stripped the **Kohinoor** and Peacock Throne from **Muhammad Shah 'Rangeela'**; **Ahmad Shah Abdali** raided repeatedly. The empire shrank to Delhi before 1857's end.
### Quick revision
- Babur: Panipat 1526 → Khanwa 1527; Baburnama in Turkish. Humayun: Chausa 1539, Kannauj 1540.
- Sher Shah: rupiya, GT road + sarais, patta-qabuliyat; Sasaram tomb.
- Akbar: 2nd Panipat (Hemu), Todar Mal's dahsala, zat-sawar mansab, Din-i-Ilahi 1582, jizya abolished, Fatehpur Sikri.
- Jahangir-Roe; Shah Jahan-Peacock Throne/Taj; Aurangzeb-jizya 1679, Tegh Bahadur 1675.
- 1739 Nadir Shah (Karnal) under Muhammad Shah 'Rangeela'.

tricks.title: Guru order — "Nana Aur Amar Ram Arjun, Har-Har-Har Tegh Gobind"
tricks.body: **N**anak, **A**ngad, **Amar** Das, **Ram** Das, **Arjan** → the three Hars (**Har**gobind, **Har** Rai, **Har** Krishan) → **Tegh** Bahadur → **Gobind** Singh.

tricks.title: Chauth vs Sardeshmukhi
tricks.body: **Ch**auth = **Ch**aar ana in the rupee (**1/4**); **Sardeshmukhi = 10%** — the Sardeshmukh claimed a 'tenth' as hereditary head.

mistakes: Adi Granth compiled by **Guru Arjan Dev**; Khalsa founded by **Guru Gobind Singh**.
Guru Arjan was executed by **Jahangir**; Guru Tegh Bahadur by **Aurangzeb**.
Third Panipat winner = **Ahmad Shah Abdali (Durrani)**, not Nadir Shah (who invaded in 1739).
subtopics.notes:
### Shivaji builds a kingdom
**Shivaji** (born 1630 at **Shivneri**; father Shahaji, mother **Jijabai**) carved a state out of Bijapur's Deccan with hill forts and light cavalry: Torna, Rajgad, Sinhagad (where **Tanaji Malusare** fell — 'the fort is won, but the lion is lost'). He killed Bijapur general **Afzal Khan** at **Pratapgarh (1659)**, raided Surat, and humbled Shaista Khan at Pune. **Jai Singh's** pressure forced the **Treaty of Purandar (1665)** — ceding 23 of his forts — and the Agra visit-escape (1666). In **1674** he was crowned **Chhatrapati** at **Raigad** (rituals by Gaga Bhatt). His **Ashtapradhan** (eight ministers) ran the state: **Peshwa** (prime), Senapati, Amatya (finance), Sachiv, Mantri, Nyayadhish, Panditrao, Sumant (foreign affairs). Revenue used **kathi assessment**; the army was paid in cash, forts were the backbone.

### The Peshwas and the confederacy
Balaji Vishwanath (first Peshwa, 1713) won back Maratha rights from the weak Mughals; his son **Baji Rao I** (1720–40) carried Maratha arms to Malwa, Bundelkhand and Delhi's gates; **Balaji Baji Rao** saw the disaster at the **Third Battle of Panipat (1761)**, where **Ahmad Shah Abdali** crushed the Marathas. Power then lay with the confederacy houses: **Scindia (Gwalior), Holkar (Indore), Gaekwad (Baroda), Bhonsle (Nagpur)** under the Peshwa at Pune. The three **Anglo-Maratha wars** — the first ended by the **Treaty of Salbai (1782)**; the second began when **Baji Rao II** signed the **Treaty of Bassein (1802)** (subsidiary alliance); the third (1817–18) ended Maratha power.

### The ten Sikh Gurus
**Guru Nanak** (born 1469 at **Talwandi**, now Nankana Sahib) preached one God, **langar** (community kitchen) and honest work. **Angad** (the **Gurmukhi** script), **Amar Das**, **Ram Das** (founded Amritsar), **Arjan Dev** (compiled the **Adi Granth**; executed 1606 by Jahangir), **Hargobind** (Miri-Piri, the armed saint), **Har Rai**, **Har Krishan**, **Tegh Bahadur** (executed 1675 by Aurangzeb), and **Guru Gobind Singh** — who created the **Khalsa** at **Anandpur Sahib on Baisakhi 1699**, the five K's, and declared the **Granth** the Guru eternal. **Banda Bahadur** carried the Khalsa fight (executed 1716); the **misls** (confederacies) ended with **Maharaja Ranjit Singh** (Sukerchakia misl) taking **Lahore (1799)** and ruling Punjab till 1839.

### Quick revision
- Shivaji: Pratapgarh-Afzal Khan (1659), Purandar (1665, Jai Singh), Agra escape (1666), coronation 1674 (Raigad, Chhatrapati).
- Ashtapradhan: Peshwa first among eight; Sumant = foreign affairs.
- Peshwa ladder: Balaji Vishwanath → Baji Rao I → Balaji Baji Rao (Panipat 1761); Salbai 1782, Bassein 1802.
- Gurus: Nanak (Talwandi) → Arjan (Adi Granth, 1606) → Tegh Bahadur (1675) → Gobind (Khalsa 1699).
- After Gobind Singh: Banda Bahadur (1716), misls, Ranjit Singh (Lahore 1799).

subtopics.notes:
### Two roads to the same God
The **Bhakti** and **Sufi** movements of the medieval centuries answered ritual-heavy religion with love, devotion and the people's languages — and quietly attacked caste.

### Bhakti in the south first
The **Alvars** (devotees of **Vishnu**) and **Nayanars** (devotees of **Shiva**) sang between the 6th and 9th centuries; the **Tevaram** hymns belong to the Nayanars (Appar, Sambandar, Sundarar); **Andal** is the woman Alvar. Philosophically, **Shankaracharya** taught **Advaita** (non-dualism), **Ramanuja** **Vishishtadvaita** (qualified non-dualism), **Madhva** **Dvaita** (dualism), Vallabhacharya **Shuddhadvaita**.

### The north Indian wave
**Ramananda** (Varanasi) opened bhakti to all castes; his disciples included **Kabir** and Ravidas. **Kabir**, the weaver of Varanasi/Benares, mocked ritual on both sides and preached nirguna bhakti — his sayings live in the **Bijak**. **Guru Nanak** founded what became Sikhism (langar, honest labour, one God). **Tulsidas** gave Rama-bhakti in **Awadhi** (*Ramcharitmanas*); **Suras** sang Krishna in **Braj** (*Sursagar*); **Mirabai** sang for Krishna; **Tukaram's abhangas** (Marathi) belong to the **Varkari** sect worshipping **Vithoba at Pandharpur** (Namdev too); **Chaitanya** swept **Bengal-Odisha** with kirtans; Shankaradeva carried Vaishnavism to Assam.

### Sufism — Islamic mysticism
Sufi orders are **silsilas** ('chains' of master-to-disciple succession); the relationship is **pir-murid**; practice includes **zikr** (recitation) and **sama** (musical gatherings — the root of qawwali). The four main Indian silsilas:
- **Chishti** — the Indian chain began with **Khwaja Moinuddin Chishti** (Ajmer), through Qutbuddin Bakhtiyar Kaki, **Baba Farid**, **Nizamuddin Auliya** (Delhi) and Nasiruddin Chiragh; it avoided the court and served all communities.
- **Suhrawardi** — **Bahauddin Zakariya** (Multan), accepted state service.
- **Naqshbandi** — **Sheikh Ahmad Sirhindi** (revivalist).
- **Qadiri** — Sufism's oldest order, later Dara Shikoh's inclination.
Saints' tombs became **dargahs** — pilgrimage (ziyarat) centres.

### What they changed
Vernacular languages flowered (Bijak, Manas, abhangas), caste distinctions weakened at the level of devotional community, and bhakti-sufi shrines (Ajmer, Pandharpur, dargahs of Delhi) became shared spaces.

### Quick revision
- Alvars-Vishnu, Nayanars-Shiva; Tevaram = Nayanar hymns; Andal = woman Alvar.
- Advaita-Shankara, Vishishtadvaita-Ramanuja, Dvaita-Madhva.
- Kabir-Bijak; Tulsidas-Awadhi; Sur-Braj; Tukaram-Marathi abhangas (Varkari, Vithoba-Pandharpur); Chaitanya-Bengal.
- Silsilas: Chishti (Moinuddin → Nizamuddin), Suhrawardi (Bahauddin Zakariya), Naqshbandi (Sirhindi), Qadiri.
- Sama = music; pir-murid; dargah = tomb-shrine.

patterns.name: Alvars, Nayanars and the Acharyas

patterns.logic:
1. **Alvars = Vishnu**, **Nayanars = Shiva**; Tevaram = Nayanar hymns (Appar, Sambandar, Sundarar); Andal = woman Alvar.
2. Schools: **Advaita-Shankaracharya, Vishishtadvaita-Ramanuja, Dvaita-Madhva**, Shuddhadvaita-Vallabhacharya.
3. Ramanuja's school influenced South Indian Vaishnavism directly.

example.q: The **Alvars** of south India were devotees of —
example.solution: **Vishnu** — the Nayanars were the Shiva-devotee counterparts.

patterns.name: North Indian Bhakti saints ↔ sect, language, work
patterns.howToSpot: Kabir-Bijak, Tulsidas-Awadhi, Tukaram-Marathi, Chaitanya-Bengal, Varkari-Vithoba, nirguna vs saguna.
patterns.logic:
1. Language anchors: **Tulsidas-Awadhi, Sur-Braj, Tukaram & Namdev-Marathi, Chaitanya-Bengal, Kabir-sadhan mix**.
2. Works: Kabir-**Bijak**; Tulsidas-**Ramcharitmanas**; Sur-**Sursagar**.
3. Sects: **Varkari = Vithoba of Pandharpur**; nirguna (Kabir, Nanak) vs saguna (Tulsidas, Sur, Mira).

example.q: Tukaram's **abhangas** are composed in which language?
example.solution: **Marathi** — he belongs to the Varkari sect of Pandharpur.

patterns.name: Sufi silsilas ↔ founders and saints

patterns.logic:
1. **Chishti**: Moinuddin (Ajmer) → Qutbuddin Bakhtiyar Kaki → **Baba Farid** → **Nizamuddin Auliya** → Nasiruddin Chiragh.
2. **Suhrawardi-Bahauddin Zakariya (Multan)**; **Naqshbandi-Ahmad Sirhindi**; **Qadiri** = oldest.
3. Terms: **silsila = chain/order**, pir-murid, **sama = musical recital**, dargah = tomb-shrine.

example.q: The Suhrawardi silsila in India is associated with which saint?
example.solution: **Bahauddin Zakariya** of Multan — unlike the Chishtis, his order accepted state service.

patterns.name: Shared features of Bhakti and Sufi movements
patterns.howToSpot: Statement questions: caste criticism, vernacular use, guru-disciple bond, devotional equality — which statements are true.
patterns.logic:
1. Common ground: devotion above ritual, **use of people's languages**, criticism of caste, the **guru's** centrality, devotional equality.
2. Neither movement was 'anti-temple' as a whole — judge each statement, not the cliché.
3. Shared spaces: dargahs and temple towns; qawwali grew from sama.

example.q: Which was a common feature of both the Bhakti and Sufi movements?
example.solution: Use of **vernacular languages** and a devotional path open to all castes and communities.

tricks.title: Mughal chroniclers — "Abul = Ain, Badauni = Bitter"
tricks.body: **Abul** Fazl wrote the official, praising **A**kbarnama/**A**in; **B**adauni wrote the **b**itter, critical *Muntakhab*.

example.q: Which historian wrote a critical account of Akbar's religious policy?
example.solution: **B**itter → **B**adauni (*Muntakhab-ut-Tawarikh*).

tricks.title: Travellers by century
tricks.body: 11th Al-Biruni → 13th Marco Polo → 14th Ibn Battuta → 15th Conti & Abdur Razzaq → 16th Paes & Nuniz → 17th Hawkins, Roe, Bernier, Tavernier.

mistakes: Ibn Battuta was **Moroccan**, not Persian.
Humayun-nama was written by **Gulbadan Begum**, not Humayun.
Marco Polo visited the **Kakatiya** kingdom in the south, not the Delhi Sultanate.
subtopics.notes:
### Chronicles of the court
- **Sultanate histories:** **Ziauddin Barani** — *Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi* (and *Fatawa-i-Jahandari*, advice to kings); **Amir Khusrau** — the 'Parrot of India' (Persian poet, *Khamsa*, *Tughlaq Nama*); Isami's *Futuh-us-Salatin*.
- **Mughal memoirs and histories:** **Babur** — *Baburnama* in Turkish; **Gulbadan Begum** — *Humayun-nama*; **Abul Fazl** — *Akbarnama* (three volumes, the third being the **Ain-i-Akbari**, the administration gazetteer); **Jahangir** — his own *Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri*; **Abdul Hamid Lahori** — *Badshahnama (Padshahnama)* on Shah Jahan.
These histories are court-centred: they praise patrons, so their numbers and claims need cross-checking with coins, inscriptions, architecture and the independent view of foreign travellers. Barani, for instance, writes as an orthodox critic of MBT's policies — useful, but angled.

### The travellers' ladder
| Traveller | From | Visited | Note |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Marco Polo** | Venice | Pandya coast (1290s) | 'Pearl fishery' accounts |
| **Ibn Battuta** | Morocco | MBT's Delhi (as qazi) | Book: *Rihla* |
| **Nicolo Conti** | Venice | Vijayanagara (Deva Raya I) | — |
| **Abdur Razzaq** | Persia (Timurid) | Vijayanagara (Deva Raya II) | Hampi's splendour |
| **Athanasius Nikitin** | Russia | Bahmani kingdom | *Voyage to India* |
| **Domingo Paes / Duarte Barbosa** | Portugal | Krishnadevaraya's court | Bazaars of Hampi |
| **Ralph Fitch** | England | Akbar's reign (1583) | First English merchant |
| **William Hawkins / Thomas Roe** | England | Jahangir's court | Roe = James I's ambassador (1615) |
| **Tavernier, Bernier, Manucci** | France/Italy | Mughal India (17th c.) | Diamond trade; Peacock Throne |

### Vernacular classics of the age
**Malik Muhammad Jayasi's Padmavat** (Awadhi Sufi romance), Sur's Braj poetry, Tulsidas' Awadhi *Manas*, Tukaram's Marathi abhangas, and Krishnadevaraya's Telugu **Amuktamalyada** — the medieval literary map is multilingual, and each classic doubles as a social source: the *Padmavat* for Sufi storytelling, the *Ain* for prices and regulations, *Rihla* for daily Delhi under MBT.

### What each source is best for
- **Administration:** the **Ain-i-Akbari** (mansabs, provinces, prices) and Sher Shah's revenue papers referenced by later writers.
- **Daily life and courts:** **Ibn Battuta's Rihla**, Paes' Hampi bazaars, Bernier's Delhi and the Peacock Throne.
- **Trade:** Tavernier on diamonds, Marco Polo on the pearl fishery, Nikitin on Bahmani markets.
- **Court politics:** Barani for the Tughlaqs, Badauni's *Muntakhab-ut-Tawarikh* (an orthodox critic of Akbar) against Abul Fazl's praise — read both ends.

### Quick revision
- Barani-*Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi*; Abul Fazl-*Akbarnama* (Ain = vol. 3); Lahori-*Badshahnama*; Babur-Turkish memoir.
- Travellers: Marco Polo-Pandya; Ibn Battuta-MBT (*Rihla*); Conti & Paes-Vijayanagara; Razzaq-Deva Raya II; Nikitin-Bahmani; Fitch-Akbar; Roe-Jahangir.
- Jayasi-*Padmavat* (Awadhi); Khusrau wrote chiefly in Persian.
- Court histories are partisan — the exam often asks 'who visited whom', so memorise the ladder.

patterns.name: Chronicle ↔ author (Sultanate and Mughal)
patterns.howToSpot: 'Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi was written by', who wrote Badshahnama, Ain-i-Akbari as part of Akbarnama.
patterns.logic:
1. Sultanate: **Barani-Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi (+ Fatawa-i-Jahandari)**; Khusrau-Persian poet (*Tughlaq Nama*).
2. Mughal: Babur-*Baburnama* (Turkish); Abul Fazl-*Akbarnama* (Ain = vol. 3); Lahori-*Badshahnama*; Gulbadan-*Humayun-nama*.
3. Match emperor to historian before answering match-the-column.

example.q: The *Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi*, a history of the Tughlaq age, was written by —
example.solution: **Ziauddin Barani**, who also wrote the political guide *Fatawa-i-Jahandari*.

patterns.name: Foreign travellers ↔ the courts they visited
patterns.howToSpot: 'Ibn Battuta came from', 'Abdur Razzaq visited whose court', Marco Polo in the Pandya kingdom, Roe-Jahangir.
patterns.logic:
1. The ladder: Marco Polo-Pandya; **Ibn Battuta-MBT (Rihla)**; Conti-Vijayanagara (Deva Raya I); **Razzaq-Deva Raya II**; Nikitin-Bahmani; Paes-Krishnadevaraya; **Fitch-Akbar; Roe-Jahangir**.
2. Ibn Battuta = **Morocco**, served as Delhi's **qazi**.
3. Roe's embassy (1615) opened English trade — a recurring 'why' question.

example.q: Who visited the court of **Deva Raya II** of Vijayanagara as an envoy of Persia?
example.solution: **Abdur Razzaq** — his account praises Hampi's wealth.

patterns.name: Regional and vernacular classics of the medieval age
patterns.howToSpot: Padmavat-Jayasi, Khusrau's language, Amuktamalyada, Humayun-nama by Gulbadan Begum.
patterns.logic:
1. **Jayasi's Padmavat** — Awadhi Sufi romance; Khusrau wrote chiefly **Persian**.
2. **Gulbadan Begum** (Humayun's sister) wrote the *Humayun-nama* — a rare woman chronicler.
3. Krishnadevaraya's *Amuktamalyada* = Telugu court classic.

example.q: **Padmavat**, the Awadhi Sufi romance of Alauddin and Padmini, was written by —
example.solution: **Malik Muhammad Jayasi** (1540).

patterns.name: Mughal court literature and autobiographies
patterns.howToSpot: 'Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri is an autobiography of', Baburnama language, Ain-i-Akbari's place in Akbarnama, Badshahnama author.
patterns.logic:
1. Two royal autobiographies: **Babur (Baburnama, Turkish)** and **Jahangir (Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri)**.
2. **Ain-i-Akbari = third volume of Akbarnama** (Abul Fazl) — administration, provinces, foods, regulations.
3. **Abdul Hamid Lahori** chronicled Shah Jahan (*Badshahnama*).

example.q: The **Ain-i-Akbari** is which part of Abul Fazl's Akbarnama?
example.solution: The **third volume** — the administrative gazetteer of Akbar's empire.

pyqPatterns.pattern: Delhi Sultanate: sultan ↔ reform or act
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Which sultan introduced the tanka', market reforms, iqta, experiments of MBT, welfare works of Firoz Shah.
pyqPatterns.approach: Map every reform to its sultan: Iltutmish (tanka-jital, Forty), Balban (sijda-paibos), Alauddin (markets, chehra-daag, Siri), MBT (Daulatabad, token currency), Firoz Shah (canals, jizya on Brahmanas). Check dynasty order when an option mixes reigns.

example.q: Which Delhi Sultan introduced the silver tanka and copper jital?
example.solution: Iltutmish — the currency reform of the Slave dynasty's consolidator.

pyqPatterns.pattern: Mughal rulers ↔ battles, orders and monuments
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Panipat-Khanwa-Chausa chain, Akbar's administration, Roe's embassy, Taj/Peacock Throne, Aurangzeb's acts.
pyqPatterns.approach: Battles: Panipat 1526 (Babur-Lodi), Khanwa 1527 (Babur-Rana Sanga), Chausa/Kannauj 1539-40 (Sher Shah-Humayun), 2nd Panipat 1556 (Akbar-Hemu). Reforms: Todar Mal's dahsala, zat-sawar. Monuments: Taj (Shah Jahan-Mumtaz), Peacock Throne. Aurangzeb: jizya 1679, Tegh Bahadur 1675.

example.q: In the Battle of Haldighati (1576), the Mughal army was commanded by:
example.solution: Raja Man Singh (of Amber), fighting Maharana Pratap.

pyqPatterns.pattern: Bhakti-Sufi saints ↔ sect, work and language
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Saint-work-language triple matching (Tulsidas-Awadhi, Kabir-Bijak, Khusrau-Nizamuddin), silsila identification.
pyqPatterns.approach: Anchors: Kabir-Bijak, Tulsidas-Ramcharitmanas (Awadhi), Tukaram-abhangas (Marathi, Varkari), Chaitanya-Bengal, Khusrau-Persian (Nizamuddin's disciple). Silsilas: Chishti (Moinuddin-Ajmer, Nizamuddin-Delhi), Suhrawardi (Bahauddin Zakariya-Multan).

example.q: Amir Khusrau, the 'Parrot of India', was a disciple of which Sufi saint?
example.solution: Nizamuddin Auliya of the Chishti order (Delhi).

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Who came from Morocco', which court a traveller saw, order of visits, books like Rihla and Si-yu-ki.
pyqPatterns.approach: Ladder: Marco Polo-Pandya, Ibn Battuta-MBT (Rihla), Conti-Vijayanagara (Deva Raya I), Razzaq-Deva Raya II, Nikitin-Bahmani, Paes-Krishnadevaraya, Fitch-Akbar, Roe-Jahangir, Tavernier-Bernier-later Mughals.

example.q: Which traveller–ruler pair is NOT correctly matched?
example.solution: Test each pair against the ladder; the mismatched one (e.g. pairing Ibn Battuta with a Vijayanagara king) is the answer.

pyqPatterns.pattern: Sikh Gurus in order and Khalsa facts
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Who compiled the Adi Granth', birthplace of Nanak, Khalsa 1699, execution years of Arjan and Tegh Bahadur.
pyqPatterns.approach: Chain: Nanak (Talwandi) → Angad (Gurmukhi) → ... → Arjan (Adi Granth, 1606) → Hargobind (Miri-Piri) → Tegh Bahadur (1675) → Gobind Singh (Khalsa, Baisakhi 1699, Anandpur; Granth as Guru).

example.q: The Khalsa was founded at Anandpur Sahib in 1699 by:
example.solution: Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth Guru, on Baisakhi day.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Gangaikonda' title, Brihadeshwara builder, Srivijaya expedition, kudavolai village elections.
pyqPatterns.approach: Vijayalaya (founder, 850) → Rajaraja I (Brihadeshwara Thanjavur) → Rajendra I (Gangaikondacholapuram, navy vs Srivijaya). Uttaramerur inscriptions (Parantaka I) = kudavolai elections, variyam committees, ur-sabha-nagaram.

example.q: Which Chola ruler sent a naval expedition against Srivijaya?
example.solution: Rajendra I — to protect the China trade route.

pyqPatterns.pattern: Vijayanagara ↔ Bahmani: founders, dynasties, five sultanates
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Founders and dates (1336 Hampi, 1347 Gulbarga), Krishnadevaraya's court, five sultanates and their houses, Talikota 1565.
pyqPatterns.approach: Vijayanagara: Harihara-Bukka (Sangama) → Saluva → Tuluva (Krishnadevaraya) → Aravidu (Rama Raya). Bahmani: Hasan Gangu; heirs Bijapur (Adil Shahi), Ahmadnagar (Nizam Shahi), Golconda (Qutb Shahi), Berar (Imad Shahi), Bidar (Barid Shahi). Talikota 1565 ends the empire.

example.q: The Battle of Talikota (1565) was fought between Vijayanagara and:
example.solution: A coalition of the five Deccan sultanates; Rama Raya was executed after the defeat.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Ashtapradhan portfolios, Peshwa line, confederacy house ↔ seat, Anglo-Maratha war treaties.
pyqPatterns.approach: Ashtapradhan: Peshwa (prime), Sumant (foreign), Amatya (finance), Senapati (army). Peshwas: Balaji Vishwanath → Baji Rao I → Balaji Baji Rao. Houses: Scindia-Gwalior, Holkar-Indore, Gaekwad-Baroda, Bhonsle-Nagpur. Salbai 1782 ends 1st war; Bassein 1802 begins 2nd.

example.q: In Shivaji's Ashtapradhan, the minister in charge of foreign affairs was the:
example.solution: Sumant (also called Dabir) — the Peshwa headed the council as prime minister.

solvedExamples.q:
Arrange the following battles in chronological order:
1. Battle of Talikota
2. Second Battle of Panipat
3. First Battle of Tarain
4. Battle of Haldighati
solvedExamples.solution: Tarain I = **1191**; Panipat II = **1556**; Talikota = **1565**; Haldighati = **1576**. So the order is 3 → 2 → 1 → 4.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Only 3 can come first (12th century) → options A, B, D remain; 1556 < 1565 puts Panipat II before Talikota → A.

solvedExamples.q: Which of the following traveller–ruler pairs is **NOT** correctly matched?
solvedExamples.solution: Abdur Razzaq, the envoy of the Timurid ruler Shah Rukh, visited **Deva Raya II** (1440s). The Portuguese **Domingo Paes** is the visitor linked with Krishnadevaraya. The other three pairs are correct.
solvedExamples.shortcut: 15th-century Persian envoy ≠ 16th-century king — the dates alone expose the wrong pair.

solvedExamples.q: The **Mansabdari** system, in which every officer held a rank defined by *zat* and *sawar*, was introduced by —
solvedExamples.solution: **Akbar** introduced the Mansabdari system (1570s). *Zat* fixed the personal rank and salary; *sawar* fixed the number of horsemen to be maintained. Mansabdars were usually paid through **jagirs**.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Mansab = rank → Akbar built the Mughal bureaucracy; Babur and Humayun had no time to.

solvedExamples.q: In Shivaji's **Ashtapradhan**, the minister in charge of **foreign affairs** was the —
solvedExamples.solution: The **Sumant (Dabir)** handled foreign affairs and relations with other states. Amatya = finance/accounts; Sachiv = royal correspondence; Panditrao = religious affairs.

practice.q: The **tripartite struggle** among the Palas, Gurjara-Pratiharas and Rashtrakutas was fought for control over —
practice.solution: From the 8th to the 10th century the three powers fought for **Kannauj**, the symbol of supremacy over north India after Harsha.

practice.q: Prithviraj Chauhan was defeated and the way to Turkish rule in north India was opened at the **Second Battle of Tarain (1192)**. Who won that battle?
practice.solution: **Muhammad Ghori** (Muizzuddin Muhammad bin Sam), beaten in 1191, returned in 1192 and defeated Prithviraj. Mahmud of Ghazni had died in 1030; Aibak was Ghori's general.

practice.q: Which Delhi Sultan introduced the silver **tanka** and the copper **jital**?
practice.solution: **Iltutmish** issued the standard Arabic coins — silver tanka and copper jital — and also organised the **iqta** system and the Group of Forty.

practice.q: The Persian court customs of **sijda** (prostration) and **paibos** (kissing the monarch's feet) were introduced by —
practice.solution: **Balban** raised the prestige of the crown with sijda, paibos and the Nauroz festival, and followed a policy of 'blood and iron'.

practice.q: Price control in the markets of Delhi, supervised by the **Shahna-i-Mandi**, was a reform of —
practice.solution: **Alauddin Khalji** fixed prices of grain, cloth, horses and slaves so that he could pay a large standing army in cash. He also started **dagh** and **chehra**.

practice.q: Which Sultan shifted his capital from Delhi to **Daulatabad (Devagiri)** in 1327?
practice.solution: **Muhammad bin Tughlaq** moved the capital to Daulatabad to control the Deccan, but soon had to return. He also issued the unsuccessful **token currency**.

practice.q: The city of **Agra** was founded in 1504 by —
practice.solution: **Sikandar Lodi** founded Agra and made it his second capital. He also introduced the **Gaz-i-Sikandari**, a standard measuring yard.

practice.q: The Telugu work ***Amuktamalyada*** was written by which Vijayanagara ruler?
practice.solution: **Krishnadevaraya** (Tuluva dynasty) wrote *Amuktamalyada*, about the Alvar saint Andal. His court had the eight poets called **Ashtadiggajas**.

practice.q: The **Battle of Talikota**, after which the city of Vijayanagara was sacked, was fought in —
practice.solution: In **January 1565** the combined forces of Bijapur, Ahmadnagar, Golconda and Bidar defeated Vijayanagara; Rama Raya was killed. 1526 and 1556 are the first two Panipats; 1576 is Haldighati.

practice.q: The silver coin called **rupiya** was first introduced by —
practice.solution: **Sher Shah Suri** (1540–45) issued the silver rupiya and the copper dam, which the Mughals continued. He also rebuilt the Grand Trunk Road.

practice.q: In the **Battle of Haldighati (1576)**, the Mughal army that fought Maharana Pratap was commanded by —
practice.solution: **Raja Man Singh** of Amber led Akbar's army at Haldighati. Bairam Khan was Akbar's regent at Panipat II; Todar Mal was the revenue expert.
practice.shortcut: Haldighati = Rajput vs Rajput: Pratap vs **Man Singh**.

practice.q: ***Ain-i-Akbari***, the detailed account of Akbar's administration, was written by —
practice.solution: **Abul Fazl** wrote the *Akbarnama*, whose third volume is the *Ain-i-Akbari*. Faizi was his brother (poet); Badauni wrote the critical *Muntakhab-ut-Tawarikh*.

practice.q: The **Khalsa** was founded at Anandpur Sahib in 1699 by —
practice.solution: **Guru Gobind Singh**, the tenth Guru, founded the Khalsa on Baisakhi 1699 and later declared the Granth Sahib the eternal Guru.
practice.shortcut: The **last** Guru created the **last** big institution — Khalsa.

practice.q: In the **Third Battle of Panipat (1761)**, the Marathas were defeated by —
practice.solution: **Ahmad Shah Abdali (Durrani)** of Afghanistan defeated the Maratha army under **Sadashivrao Bhau** on 14 January 1761. Nadir Shah invaded in 1739 and Timur in 1398.

practice.q: The traveller **Ibn Battuta**, who served as qazi of Delhi under Muhammad bin Tughlaq, came from —
practice.solution: **Ibn Battuta** was from **Tangier, Morocco**. He reached India in 1333 and described it in his travel book *Rihla*.

practice.q: Tulsidas composed the ***Ramcharitmanas*** in which language?
practice.solution: *Ramcharitmanas* (16th century) is in **Awadhi**. Surdas wrote *Sursagar* in Braj Bhasha; Vidyapati wrote in Maithili.

practice.q: **Amir Khusrau**, the poet called *Tuti-i-Hind*, was a disciple of which Sufi saint?
practice.solution: Amir Khusrau was the devoted disciple of **Nizamuddin Auliya** of the Chishti order in Delhi; both are buried in the Nizamuddin dargah complex. Bahauddin Zakariya was a Suhrawardi saint of Multan; Sirhindi was Naqshbandi.
practice.shortcut: Both are in Delhi's **Nizamuddin** — the disciple rests beside his master.

practice.q: The founder of the **Pala dynasty** of Bengal, said to have been elected by the people, was —
practice.solution: **Gopala** (c. 750) was chosen as king by the people to end anarchy — a rare elected foundation in Indian history.

practice.q: **Nagabhata I**, who repelled Arab invaders, was a ruler of which dynasty?
practice.solution: **Nagabhata I** of the **Gurjara-Pratihara** dynasty (Avanti-Malwa) checked the Arab advance from Sind; the Pratiharas later held Kannauj.

practice.q: The imperial **Chola** dynasty's line at Thanjavur began with —
practice.solution: **Vijayalaya** captured Thanjavur (c. 850) and founded the imperial line; Rajaraja I and Rajendra I carried it to its height.

practice.q: The **Brihadeshwara (Rajarajeshwara) temple** at Thanjavur was built by —
practice.solution: **Rajaraja I** built the Brihadeshwara temple (c. 1010) — a UNESCO-listed masterpiece of Dravida architecture with a 13-storey vimana.

practice.q: Rajendra I took the title **'Gangaikonda'** after —
options: A march to the river Ganga
practice.solution: 'Gangaikonda' = 'bringer of the Ganga' — after his northward march to the Ganga; he then built **Gangaikondacholapuram** as a new capital.

practice.q: The Chola village committees chosen under the **kudavolai** system were called —
practice.solution: The elected committees were called **variyams** (e.g. garden, tank, justice committees). 'Ur', 'sabha' and 'nagaram' are the types of village assemblies.

practice.q: The **Uttaramerur inscriptions**, which detail Chola village elections, belong to the reign of —
practice.solution: The Uttaramerur records of village committee elections date to **Parantaka I**'s reign (10th century) — earlier than the famous imperial pair.

practice.q: In Chola administration, the assembly of a **Brahmadeya** (Brahmana-grant) village was called the —
practice.solution: **Sabha** = assembly of Brahmadeya villages; **ur** = ordinary villages; **nagaram** = market/merchant towns. The sabha's working is the best documented (Uttaramerur).

practice.q: The **Konark Sun Temple** was built by —
practice.solution: **Narasimhadeva I** of the **Eastern Ganga** dynasty built Konark (13th century) — a chariot-shaped Sun temple, a UNESCO site.

practice.q: The **Hoysala** capital **Dorasamudra** is today known as —
practice.solution: Dorasamudra is modern **Halebidu** (Karnataka); the Hoysaleswara temple stands there, and Belur's Chennakeshava temple is nearby.

practice.q: **Prithviraj Chauhan** ruled from Delhi and —
practice.solution: The Chauhan kingdom had two centres — **Delhi and Ajmer**. Jaichand's Gahadavalas held Kannauj.

practice.q:
Consider the statements:
1. The Cholas traded actively with Song China.
2. Chola bronzes are famous for the Nataraja form.
3. The Chola land survey formed the basis of the revenue assessment.
Which are correct?
practice.solution: All three are standard Chola facts: embassies and trade with Song China, the superb **Nataraja bronzes**, and a careful land survey for revenue.
practice.shortcut: Chola administration + trade + art — all three usually appear together as true statements.

practice.q: Who is regarded as the **real consolidator** of the Delhi Sultanate among the Slave rulers?
practice.solution: **Iltutmish** (1211–1236) saved the infant state from rivals, organised the iqta system, issued tanka-jital and formed the Chahalgani.
practice.shortcut: Aibak founded, Iltutmish consolidated, Balban dignified.

practice.q: The **first and only woman** to rule Delhi was —
practice.solution: **Razia** (1236–1240), daughter of Iltutmish, was the first and only woman sultan of Delhi.

practice.q: Under the **iqta system**, the holder of the iqta was expected mainly to —
options: Stay at court as a hostage
Collect revenue and maintain troops for the Sultan
practice.solution: The **muqti** collected the assigned revenue and kept a fixed body of troops for royal service — revenue assignment for service, not land ownership.

practice.q: Alauddin Khalji identified horses by **branding (daag)** and soldiers by —
practice.solution: **Chehra** (descriptive roll of the soldier) and **daag** (branding of horses) were Alauddin's tools to stop the ghost-soldier fraud in his standing army.

practice.q: Which Sultan shifted his court's perception of royal dignity by enforcing **sijda and paibos**?
practice.solution: **Balban** introduced Persian court customs — **sijda** (prostration) and **paibos** (kissing the feet) — to overawe the nobles with royal majesty.

practice.q: **Firoz Shah Tughlaq** is remembered for all of the following EXCEPT —
practice.solution: The **token currency** was Muhammad bin Tughlaq's failed experiment. Firoz Shah built canals, charity institutions and extended jizya.

practice.q: **Timur's** invasion, which crippled the Delhi Sultanate, took place in —
practice.solution: **Timur** sacked Delhi in **1398**; the Tughlaqs never recovered, and the **Sayyid** dynasty (Khizr Khan) followed.

practice.q: Bakhtiyar Khalji's destruction of the great Buddhist monasteries of **Bihar** happened during —
practice.solution: Ikhtiyaruddin **Bakhtiyar Khalji** swept through Bihar and Bengal in the early 1200s (Aibak's period), destroying Nalanda, Odantapuri and Vikramashila's remnants.

practice.q: **Vijayanagara** was founded in 1336 by —
practice.solution: The Sangama brothers **Harihara and Bukka** founded Vijayanagara at Hampi in **1336**, guided by the guru **Vidyaranya**.

practice.q: Which dynasty did **Krishnadevaraya** belong to?
practice.solution: Krishnadevaraya was the greatest ruler of the **Tuluva** dynasty (1509–1529), the third of Vijayanagara's four houses.

practice.q: Krishnadevaraya wrote the Telugu classic **Amuktamalyada** on —
options: Devotion to God (Andal's story) and governance
practice.solution: *Amuktamalyada* (in Telugu) tells the story of the Vaishnava saint **Andal** and also contains Krishnadevaraya's famous sections on **governance**.
practice.shortcut: His book = Amuktamalyada; his title = Andhra Bhoja.

practice.q: Which Portuguese traveller left a vivid account of **Krishnadevaraya's** Vijayanagara?
practice.solution: **Domingo Paes** (and Duarte Barbosa) visited Vijayanagara in Krishnadevaraya's time and praised its bazaars and grandeur. Nikitin came to the Bahmani kingdom earlier; Ibn Battuta to the Sultanate.

practice.q: The title **'Andhra Bhoja'** was earned by —
practice.solution: **Krishnadevaraya** was called 'Andhra Bhoja' for his patronage of Telugu letters (like the great Bhoja).

practice.q: The **Bahmani kingdom** was founded in 1347 by —
practice.solution: **Alauddin Hasan Bahman Shah (Hasan Gangu)** founded the Bahmani kingdom in 1347, with the capital at Gulbarga.

practice.q: The five sultanates born from the Bahmani breakup include **Berar**, ruled by the —
practice.solution: Five heirs: **Bijapur (Adil Shahi), Ahmadnagar (Nizam Shahi), Golconda (Qutb Shahi), Berar (Imad Shahi), Bidar (Barid Shahi)**.

practice.q: The ruined city of **Hampi**, capital of Vijayanagara, stands on the bank of the —
practice.solution: Hampi sits on the **Tungabhadra** (a Krishna tributary); the site is a UNESCO World Heritage property.

practice.q: The **Raichur doab**, long contested between Vijayanagara and the Bahmanis, lies between the rivers —
practice.solution: The doab (land between two rivers) of the **Krishna and Tungabhadra** was the empire's bone of contention — won decisively at the Battle of Raichur (1520).

practice.q: At the Battle of Talikota, Vijayanagara faced a coalition of —
practice.solution: In 1565 the five successor sultanates (Bijapur, Ahmadnagar, Golconda, Berar, Bidar) united at **Talikota (Rakshasa-Tangadi)**, crushed Vijayanagara and executed Rama Raya.
practice.shortcut: Talikota = five heirs of Bahmani united.

practice.q: In the **Battle of Khanwa (1527)**, Babur defeated —
practice.solution: **Khanwa (1527)**: Babur beat the Rajput confederacy of **Rana Sanga** of Mewar; Panipat (1526) had already finished Ibrahim Lodi.

practice.q: Babur wrote his memoirs, the **Tuzuk-i-Baburi (Baburnama)**, in —
practice.solution: The Baburnama is in **Chagatai Turkish**, Babur's mother tongue (it was later translated into Persian).

practice.q: Humayun lost his empire to Sher Shah at the battles of **Chausa** and —
practice.solution: **Chausa (1539)** and **Kannauj (Bilgram, 1540)** — both against Sher Khan (Sher Shah Sur); Humayun then wandered 15 years.

practice.q: **Din-i-Ilahi**, the syncretic creed, was promulgated by —
practice.solution: **Akbar** announced Din-i-Ilahi in **1582** as a discipleship order of sulh-i-kul (universal peace); Birbal was its most famous acceptor.

practice.q: The **Second Battle of Panipat (1556)** was won by Akbar's forces against —
practice.solution: Regent **Bairam Khan** led the young Akbar's army against **Hemu**, the wazir of the Surs, who had taken Delhi; Hemu was struck down and killed.

practice.q: In the **mansabdari** system, 'zat' fixed personal rank and pay; 'sawar' fixed —
practice.solution: **Zat** = personal rank and pay; **sawar** = number of horsemen the mansabdar had to maintain.

practice.q: The **Taj Mahal** was built by Shah Jahan in memory of —
practice.solution: **Mumtaz Mahal** (Arjumand Banu Begum), Shah Jahan's wife, is commemorated by the Taj on the Yamuna at Agra.

practice.q: The jewelled **Peacock Throne (Takht-i-Taus)** was made for —
practice.solution: The **Peacock Throne** was made under **Shah Jahan** (by goldsmith Bebadal Khan) — taken away by Nadir Shah in 1739.
practice.shortcut: Peacock Throne = Shah Jahan → Nadir Shah.

practice.q: Which Mughal emperor had **Guru Tegh Bahadur** executed in 1675?
practice.solution: **Aurangzeb** executed Guru Tegh Bahadur (the 9th Sikh Guru) in Delhi in **1675**; Guru Arjan Dev had been executed under Jahangir (1606).

practice.q:
Consider the statements about the later Mughals:
1. The Sayyid brothers were called 'king-makers'.
2. Nadir Shah won the Battle of Karnal (1739).
3. The Kohinoor was taken to Persia after 1739.
Which are correct?
practice.solution: All three are standard: the **Sayyid brothers** placed and removed emperors, **Karnal (1739)** opened Delhi to Nadir Shah, and the **Kohinoor** (with the Peacock Throne) went to Persia.
practice.shortcut: Later-Mughal misery in one chain: Sayyids → Karnal → loot.

practice.q: Shivaji was formally crowned **Chhatrapati** in 1674 at —
practice.solution: The coronation (**1674**) took place at **Raigad** fort, with the scholar Gaga Bhatt officiating.

practice.q: Which Bijapur general did Shivaji kill at **Pratapgarh (1659)**?
practice.solution: **Afzal Khan** was killed in a tiger-claw encounter at Pratapgarh; Shaista Khan (Mughal) was Shivaji's Pune adversary.

practice.q: The **Treaty of Purandar (1665)**, by which Shivaji ceded 23 forts, followed the campaign of —
practice.solution: Rajput general **Mirza Raja Jai Singh** (of Amber) besieged Purandar; the treaty led to Shivaji's Agra visit and famous escape (1666).
practice.shortcut: Purandar-Agra both trace to Jai Singh.

practice.q: In Shivaji's **Ashtapradhan**, the **Peshwa** was —
options: The prime minister and first among the eight
practice.solution: The **Peshwa** headed the eight ministers; **Senapati** led the army, **Amatya** finance, **Sumant/Dabir** foreign affairs, **Nyayadhish** justice.

practice.q: The **first Peshwa** of the Marathas was —
practice.solution: **Balaji Vishwanath** (Peshwa from 1713) founded the Peshwa line; Baji Rao I made it great; Balaji Baji Rao faced Panipat.

practice.q: The **Treaty of Salbai (1782)** concluded —
practice.solution: **Salbai (1782)**, signed under Warren Hastings, ended the **First** Anglo-Maratha War (with Nana Fadnavis' Pune regime).

practice.q:
Match the confederacy house with its seat:
1. Holkar — Indore  2. Gaekwad — Baroda  3. Bhonsle — Gwalior
Which are correct?
practice.solution: **Holkar-Indore** and **Gaekwad-Baroda** are right; **Bhonsle ruled Nagpur**, while **Gwalior** belonged to the **Scindias**.

practice.q: Guru Nanak was born in 1469 at —
practice.solution: **Talwandi** (Rai Bhoe di Talwandi, now **Nankana Sahib** in Pakistan) is Guru Nanak's birthplace.

practice.q: The policy of **Miri-Piri** (temporal and spiritual authority), symbolised by two swords, belongs to —
practice.solution: **Guru Hargobind** (6th Guru) wore two swords — Miri (temporal power) and Piri (spiritual) — after his father Arjan's execution.

practice.q: The **Khalsa** was created by Guru Gobind Singh at —
practice.solution: On **Baisakhi of 1699** at **Anandpur Sahib**, Guru Gobind Singh founded the Khalsa with the Panj Pyare and the five K's.
practice.shortcut: 1699 + Baisakhi + Anandpur — all three go together.

practice.q: **Banda Bahadur**, who led the Khalsa after Guru Gobind Singh, was executed in 1716 by —
practice.solution: **Farrukh Siyar** executed Banda Bahadur at Delhi in **1716** after his capture at Gurdas Nangal.

practice.q:
Consider the statements:
1. Ranjit Singh captured Lahore in 1799.
2. The Khalsa was formed before Banda Bahadur's leadership.
3. Guru Gobind Singh named the Adi Granth as the eternal Guru.
Which are correct?
practice.solution: All three are standard: **Lahore 1799**, the **Khalsa (1699)** predating Banda Bahadur, and **1708**'s declaration of the Granth as Guru.
practice.shortcut: Chain: Khalsa 1699 → Granth-Guru 1708 → Banda → misls → Ranjit.

practice.q: The **Vishishtadvaita** (qualified non-dualism) philosophy was taught by —
practice.solution: **Ramanuja** taught Vishishtadvaita; Shankara = Advaita; Madhva = Dvaita; Vallabha = Shuddhadvaita.

practice.q: The **Tevaram** hymns are associated with —
practice.solution: The **Tevaram** is the Nayanars' Shiva-bhakti hymn collection (Appar, Sambandar, Sundarar).

practice.q: The sayings of **Kabir** are collected in the —
practice.solution: Kabir's verses live in the **Bijak** (kept by his followers) and in Sikh and Dadu panth collections.

practice.q: **Chaitanya Mahaprabhu**, the Krishna-bhakti saint, belonged to —
practice.solution: **Chaitanya** of Navadwip (Bengal) spread Krishna-bhakti through **kirtan** across Bengal and Odisha.

practice.q: The **Varkari** sect, with its pilgrim movement to Pandharpur, worships —
practice.solution: The **Varkari** pilgrims (Namdev, Tukaram, Janabai) worship **Vithoba (Vitthal)** at **Pandharpur** on the Chandrabhaga.

practice.q: The dargah of **Khwaja Moinuddin Chishti** is at —
practice.solution: **Moinuddin Chishti** settled at **Ajmer**; his dargah ('Gharib Nawaz') is India's most visited Sufi shrine.

practice.q: In Sufi practice, the musical recital of devotion is called —
practice.solution: **Sama** is the musical recital (root of qawwali); **zikr** is silent/chanted remembrance; **silsila** is the order's chain.

practice.q:
Match the silsila with its Indian anchor:
1. Naqshbandi — Ahmad Sirhindi
2. Chishti — Nizamuddin Auliya
3. Suhrawardi — Baba Farid
Which are correct?
practice.solution: **Sirhindi** anchors the Naqshbandi and **Nizamuddin** the Chishti order in Delhi; **Baba Farid** was Chishti (Pakpattan), while the **Suhrawardi** anchor is **Bahauddin Zakariya** (Multan).
practice.shortcut: Farid = Chishti, Zakariya = Suhrawardi — don't swap.

practice.q: Both Bhakti and Sufi saints chiefly communicated in —
options: The languages of the common people
practice.solution: Both movements deliberately used **vernaculars** — Awadhi, Braj, Marathi, Punjabi, Bengali, and Persian-Hindavi — to reach ordinary people.
practice.shortcut: Vernacular reach is their shared signature.

practice.q: The relation between a Sufi master and his disciple is termed —
practice.solution: In Sufism the master is the **pir** (sheikh) and the disciple the **murid**; initiation into the order creates the silsila link.

practice.q: The **Baburnama**, the first Mughal memoir, was written by Babur himself in —
practice.solution: Babur wrote in **Chagatai Turkish**; it was later rendered into Persian for the court.

practice.q: ***Badshahnama* (Padshahnama)**, the official history of Shah Jahan's reign, was written by —
practice.solution: **Abdul Hamid Lahori** compiled the *Badshahnama*; Abul Fazl wrote for Akbar and Barani for the Tughlaq age.

practice.q:
Consider the statements:
1. Barani wrote both a history and a mirror-for-princes.
2. Amir Khusrau is credited with the Tughlaq Nama.
3. Isami's Futuh-us-Salatin deals with the Bahmani court.
Which are correct?
practice.solution: Barani wrote the *Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi* and *Fatawa-i-Jahandari*; Khusrau wrote the *Tughlaq Nama*. **Isami's *Futuh-us-Salatin* is a Sultanate-Deccan verse history (Delhi Sultans), not a Bahmani court chronicle.**
practice.shortcut: Statement 3 swaps the court — check each work's subject.

practice.q: The Venetian traveller **Marco Polo** visited —
practice.solution: **Marco Polo** (1290s) travelled along the Coromandel coast, describing the Pandya pearl fishery.

practice.q: The Russian traveller **Athanasius Nikitin** visited —
practice.solution: **Nikitin** (*Voyage to India*, 15th century) travelled in the **Bahmani** kingdom; his account is a Russian classic.

practice.q: The English merchant **Ralph Fitch** travelled in India during the reign of —
practice.solution: **Ralph Fitch** (1583–91) was the first English merchant-traveller to describe Mughal India — he came in **Akbar's** reign, decades before Roe.
practice.shortcut: Fitch before the Company: Akbar's time.

practice.q: **Amir Khusrau**, the 'Parrot of India', wrote his poetry mainly in —
practice.solution: **Amir Khusrau** was the great **Persian** poet of the Sultanate (he also played with Hindavi in couplets); he served several sultans and sat at Nizamuddin Auliya's feet.

practice.q: The **Humayun-nama** was written by —
practice.solution: **Gulbadan Banu Begum**, Humayun's sister, wrote the *Humayun-nama* — a rare woman's inside view of the Mughal household.

practice.q: ***Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri*** is —
options: A biography of Jahangir by Abul Fazl
practice.solution: **Jahangir** wrote his memoirs himself (*Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri/Jahangirnama*) — as Babur had before him.

practice.q:
Consider the statements:
1. The Ain-i-Akbari records provincial administration and regulations.
2. Abul Fazl completed the Akbarnama in three volumes.
3. Badauni's Muntakhab-ut-Tawarikh is hostile to Akbar's religious policies.
Which are correct?
practice.solution: All three are standard: the **Ain** details administration, the **Akbarnama** ran to three volumes, and **Badauni** (an orthodox critic) wrote the *Muntakhab-ut-Tawarikh*.
practice.shortcut: Friendly (Abul Fazl) vs hostile (Badauni) lenses on the same reign.
